title: Egypt Falls to Babylon
sum: Chapter 46 opens the collection of oracles against the nations with Egypt, the great power to the southwest that Judah leaned on. The first poem (46:3-12) pictures Egypt's army drilling for battle, then running. The date is the battle of Carchemish on the Euphrates in 605 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon broke Pharaoh Neco's army and ended Egypt's hopes in Syria. Egypt rose like the Nile, the poem says, but the LORD has a sacrifice waiting in the north.

The second poem (46:13-26) turns to a later threat, Nebuchadnezzar's invasion of Egypt itself, and names Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes. It mocks Pharaoh as 'all noise' and ends by promising that people will live in Egypt again. A short word to Jacob (46:27-28) closes the chapter: do not be afraid.
readings: Read as history

The first poem is a poem about the 605 BC defeat at Carchemish, known from the Babylonian Chronicle. The second is about Nebuchadnezzar's attack on Egypt, which a Babylonian fragment dates to 568/567 BC, though no source says he conquered Egypt.
Read as literature
Both poems are sets of pictures: a river that floods, a heifer stung by a fly, a snake that slips away, woodcutters in a forest. They use Egypt's own images (the Nile, the Apis bull) against it.
Read as a warning to Judah
The oracles are addressed to Judah, which kept turning to Egypt for help. The rout of Egypt's army is the argument that such help will fail.

views.H: Carchemish (605 BC) is documented in the Babylonian Chronicle (BM 21946). A fragment of Nebuchadnezzar's thirty-seventh year (568/567 BC) mentions a clash with Egypt under Amasis, but it is broken and does not report a conquest. Egypt continued under Amasis until 526 BC, then fell to Persia (525 BC). The partial fulfillment is debated.
views.C: Many scholars see two poems (3-12 and 14-24) with prose frames (2, 13, 25-26) and the comfort poem (27-28) added from 30:10-11. The Greek is shorter at 46:15-17, 25-26, as the variants show. Qumran's 2QJer has parts of 46:27-28 only, and it agrees with the Masoretic Text in wording (it spells some words more fully).
views.J: Radak (Rabbi David Kimchi), as read on Sefaria, says the prophecy first concerns Pharaoh Neco's defeat at Carchemish and then turns to Nebuchadnezzar's later attack on Egypt itself (his comments on 46:2 and 46:13).
views.X: The New Testament does not quote this chapter.
views.F: Some futurist readers see 46:26 and Isaiah 19:19-25 as a promise that Egypt will turn to the LORD in a coming age; others read it as already fulfilled.

deep.b: For these four chapters the sources read were: the Masoretic Text word by word (the Leningrad Codex, from the site's word list); the Greek in Swete's edition, which prints mostly Codex Vaticanus, including its different order (Egypt at Greek 26, the Philistines at 29, Edom at 29:8-23, Ammon at 30:1-5, Kedar and Hazor at 30:6-11, Damascus at 30:12-16, Moab at 31, Elam at 25:14-19); and the Dead Sea Scrolls transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC), which shows one Qumran copy in these chapters, 2QJer (2Q13), with parts of 46:27-28, 47:1-7, 48:7, 48:25-39, 48:43-45 and 49:10 (it has nothing of 48:40-42). On this page and in these chapters "the Greek" means the text of Codex Vaticanus as Swete prints it. The Targum, Vulgate and Peshitta are cited only where named. Radak's commentary was read on Sefaria at 46:2, 46:13, 47:2 and 48:10.

deep.h: What the Greek lacks in these chapters
deep.b: The Greek is shorter throughout. In chapter 46 it lacks verse 26, much of verse 25, and the name Tahpanhes; it adds 'Neco' in verse 17. Many small items differ: 'Nebuchadnezzar', 'the prophet', 'the LORD declares', titles, and repeated words. These are too many to list singly. The variants give the places where the sense changes. Examples of the small minuses in this chapter are 'king of Babylon' at 46:13 and 'the LORD declares' at 46:23.

deep.title: Why Tabor and Carmel?
deep.b: The invader 'like Tabor among the mountains' (46:18) is the only picture in the poem that does not come from Egypt's world. This is Claude's own suggestion, and a weak one: Carmel stands at the sea and Tabor at the inland end of the Jezreel Valley, the two ends of the northern plain that Egyptian armies crossed on their way to Syria, so the poem might tell Egypt that the enemy looms over its own road. But Tabor lies off the main road, and the text gives no hint of this meaning. The plainer reading is that the two mountains simply stand for something large and sudden.

echoes: 2 Kings 23:29-35; 2 Kings 24:7; Jeremiah 30:10-11; Jeremiah 43:8-13; Jeremiah 44:1; Isaiah 19; Ezekiel 29-32; Nahum 3:8-10

settings.to: Judah, and above all the court and people of Jerusalem, who were tempted to trust in Egypt
settings.when: In or soon after the fourth year of Jehoiakim (605 BC), when Nebuchadnezzar crushed Neco's army at Carchemish (46:2)
settings.why: Jehoiakim owed his throne to Neco (2 Kings 23:34), and many in Judah looked to Egypt against Babylon. The poem shows Egypt's army beaten and tells Judah not to count on it. It also tells them the LORD, not Babylon, is the one who has done this (46:10).
settings.readers: Exiles reading the book after 586 saw proof that the prophet had been right to say that Egypt could not save them (compare 37:5-10).
views: Spoken in 605 BC
Most commentators place the oracle in the year of the battle, as 46:2 says.
A poem about a defeat that is still coming
Some read 3-12 as a mock call to arms before the battle, with the defeat seen in advance.

settings.to: Disputed: the people of Egypt in a symbolic address, Judeans in Jerusalem, or the Judean refugees who lived in Migdol, Tahpanhes and Memphis
settings.when: Not dated. Proposed occasions: the 601 BC clash between Egypt and Babylon, Apries's advance in 588 (37:5), or after 586 when Jeremiah was himself in Egypt (43-44)
settings.why: It warns that Babylon's power will reach Egypt itself, so no refuge there is safe. Jeremiah 43:8-13 gives the same message to the refugees at Tahpanhes. Verse 26 adds that Egypt will be inhabited again.
settings.readers: After 568/567 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar went to fight Egypt (a broken Babylonian tablet says so; see the note at 46:13), readers could see a partial fulfillment; the book's own readers did not see a full conquest.
views: To the refugees in Egypt
The list of Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes in 46:14 is the list in 44:1, so the oracle may belong to the same moment (Holladay and others).
A message sent out toward Egypt
Others take the verse 14 summons literally as a proclamation toward Egypt; the book gives no sign it was delivered there.

settings.to: Israel in exile, as the book's readers; the first hearers are those surrounded by Egypt's fall and Babylon's rise
settings.when: Undated; the same words are in 30:10-11
settings.why: Between oracles of doom on the nations, a word to Israel: the nations will be finished, but Israel will be disciplined, not destroyed.
settings.readers: For exiles in Babylon it was a promise that the end of Babylon's rule and their return were part of the plan.

title: The Sword and the Coast
sum: The shortest nations oracle is about the Philistines, who lived on the coastal plain of Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Gath and Ekron. A flood from the north is coming, with the thunder of horses and chariots; fathers will not turn back for their children. Tyre and Sidon's last helpers will be cut off. The prophet, or the people, cry to the sword of the LORD to rest, and the answer is that it has been given orders against Ashkelon and the coast.

The poem uses the same pictures as chapter 46 but turns them. Egypt rose like the Nile (46:7-8); now waters rise from the north (47:2). The heading says 'before Pharaoh struck Gaza', and dating it depends on which strike is meant.
readings: Read as history
The Philistine cities were attacked by Egypt and then by Babylon, who destroyed Ashkelon in 604 BC (Babylonian Chronicle), a date archaeology supports.
Read as literature
A short poem built on the flood and on the dialogue with the sword. Its last verses are a conversation: 'How long?' and the LORD's reply.

views.H: Gaza, Ashkelon, Ekron and Ashdod were rich trading cities. The Babylonian Chronicle records that Nebuchadnezzar took Ashkelon in Kislev 604 BC and turned it into ruins; the excavations by Lawrence Stager found the burned layer and a destroyed marketplace.
views.C: The Greek heading ('Against the foreigners') lacks the clause about Pharaoh, and 2QJer shares the first-person 'I will cut off' of the Greek at 47:4. This is among the clear examples where a Hebrew scroll sides with the Greek against the Masoretic Text.
views.J: Radak (Rabbi David Kimchi), as read on Sefaria, takes the waters from the north as the Chaldean army, which comes from the north and rises like a flood (his comment on 47:2).
views.X: Christian readers have used the sword of the LORD (47:6) as a picture of God's judgment on his enemies; the New Testament does not quote this chapter.
views.F: Most commentators place the oracle in antiquity and read it as fulfilled by the Babylonian campaigns on the coast.

settings.to: Judah, as neighbors of the Philistine coast; the Philistines themselves are not the hearers
settings.when: 'Before Pharaoh struck Gaza' (47:1). The Babylonian capture of Ashkelon in Kislev 604 BC fits the close of the poem (47:5-7), but no text states that
settings.why: Philistine cities were Judah's neighbors and often Egypt's allies. The oracle warns that the Babylonian flood will sweep over the coast and that no ally, not even Tyre or Sidon, can help.
settings.readers: Exiles knew that Ashkelon was destroyed in 604 BC, a sign of what Babylon would do.
views: Egypt's strike on Gaza
Herodotus says Neco took a Syrian city 'Kadytis' (taken by many to be Gaza); that was about 609 BC.
A later strike
Others place it under Psamtik II or Apries, in the years leading up to 588.

title: Moab Poured Out
sum: Moab, the plateau kingdom east of the Dead Sea, gets the longest of the nations oracles. The poem tours its towns one at a time, from Nebo and Heshbon in the north to Zoar in the south, while the people flee, mourn and howl. It charges Moab with pride and security: for generations Moab has sat undisturbed 'on its dregs' like unpoured wine, trusting its works, its treasures and its god Chemosh. Now men come to tip the jars and smash them.

Much of the poem is taken from Isaiah 15-16, and its last section reuses an old victory song from Numbers 21:28-29. In the middle the speaker weeps for Moab, as in Isaiah. The chapter ends with a promise Isaiah lacks: the LORD will turn Moab's fortunes around 'in the last days'.
readings: Read as a real lament
The weeping in 31-36 is sincere. A prophet whose book is full of lament (4:19; 9:1) can weep for a neighbor who is about to be judged.
Read as taunt
Other scholars hear irony: the lament copies funeral song to celebrate a fall. The chapter's closing promise and its harsh lines (48:10, 26) are cited on both sides.
Read as a patchwork of older songs
The poem is a collection of reused songs (Isaiah 15-16, Numbers 21 and 24, Isaiah 24) sewn together by a later editor or by Jeremiah himself.

views.H: Moab revolted against Babylon in Jehoiakim's time, then, with Edom, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon, met Zedekiah in 594/593 BC (27:3). Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar subdued Ammon and Moab in his twenty-third year (582 BC). Later Moab fades from the record.
views.C: Verses 45-47 are not in the Greek, though 2QJer has 45. The Greek is shorter in 40-41, too. The parallels with Isaiah show that either Jeremiah quoted Isaiah or both used older poems. Brian Jones's study of Isaiah 15-16 argues for irony in the Isaiah version.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition praises the weeping prophets of Israel against Balaam (Numbers Rabbah 20:1). Radak reads 48:10 as a curse on any warrior who slacks.
views.X: Christians have read Moab as a figure of pride and trust in self. The restoration of 48:47 has been read as Gentile salvation; the curse in 48:10 has been misused to justify violence.
views.F: Some Christian futurists see a literal restoration of Moab in a coming age (48:47); most read Moab's fall as fulfilled and the 'last days' as the age of the church or the age to come.

deep.b:
The Plain follows Isaiah's wording wherever the Hebrew is the same. The main parallels are below. Jeremiah rearranges and adds; the only place the two disagree in witnesses is Kir-heres (2QJer has Kir-hareseth, as Isaiah 16:7 does) and the 'we have heard' of 48:29 (2QJer has 'hear').

JeremiahParallel
Jeremiah 48:5 (the climb to Luhith; the road to Horonaim)Isaiah 15:5
Jeremiah 48:29-30 (Moab's pride)Isaiah 16:6
Jeremiah 48:31 (I howl for Moab; Kir-heres)Isaiah 16:7, 11
Jeremiah 48:32-33 (the vine of Sibmah; the harvest shout)Isaiah 16:8-10
Jeremiah 48:34 (Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz, Zoar, Nimrim)Isaiah 15:4-6
Jeremiah 48:35 (the high place)Isaiah 16:12
Jeremiah 48:36 (the heart like flutes; riches lost)Isaiah 16:11; 15:7
Jeremiah 48:37-38 (shaved heads; rooftops)Isaiah 15:2-3
Jeremiah 48:43-44 (terror, trench and trap)Isaiah 24:17-18
Jeremiah 48:45-46 (fire from Heshbon; woe to Moab)Numbers 21:28-29; 24:17

Isaiah has no verse like 48:47 (the restoration of Moab).

deep.h: Chemosh and the stone of Mesha
deep.b: Moab's national god Chemosh and its king Mesha are known to us from a basalt stone found at Dibon in 1868. Mesha says Chemosh was angry with his land and let Israel oppress it, and that Chemosh then told him to take Nebo from Israel. He lists towns he built, among them Dibon, Aroer, Kiriathaim, Beth-diblathaim and Beth-meon, and he says he dragged the vessels of the LORD from Nebo before Chemosh. Jeremiah 48 names many of the same towns, and says Chemosh himself will go out into exile (48:7). The comparison is this site's, not a claim that Jeremiah knew the stone: both texts explain a nation's fortunes by the act of its god, as many ancient Near Eastern texts do. See 2 Kings 3.

echoes: Isaiah 15-16; Isaiah 24:17-18; Numbers 21:28-29; Numbers 24:17; 2 Kings 3; Amos 2:1-3; Zephaniah 2:8-11; Jeremiah 25:21; Jeremiah 27:3

settings.by: Jeremiah, as the LORD's spokesman, in a poem that reuses older songs (Isaiah 15-16; Numbers 21:28-29; 24:17)
settings.to: Judah, as Moab's neighbor and a possible partner in rebellion against Babylon; Moab is described but not addressed as hearer
settings.when: Undated. The conspiracy of the kings of Moab, Edom, Ammon, Tyre and Sidon with Zedekiah (27:3, in 594/593 BC) is a likely setting. Josephus dates a Babylonian attack on Moab to 582 BC
settings.why: It tells Judah that Moab, at ease behind its pride, will not escape Babylon, so an alliance with it is useless. The old songs recast for the occasion remind Moab's neighbors that Moab was once an enemy that Israel had broken.
settings.readers: After the exile it served as a record that Moab's rest had ended and that the judgment was God's.
views: Written by Jeremiah
The traditional view: Jeremiah composed it, borrowing Isaiah's poem as every prophet could.
Compiled from older poems
Many critical scholars see Jeremiah's poem as a collage of older material (Isaiah 15-16 and the Numbers songs), put together later, with the promise in 47 added still later.

title: Five More Nations
sum: Chapter 49 holds five oracles in a row. Ammon is charged with taking Gad's land and promised a restoration (1-6). Edom, the longest, is told its wisdom, cliffs and pride will not save it, and it must drink the cup (7-22); much of it matches Obadiah. Damascus melts in panic (23-27). Kedar and Hazor, Arab tribes with no city walls, are plundered (28-33). Elam, far to the east, loses its bow and is scattered to the four winds, yet in the last days its fortunes are turned (34-39).
The oracles share formulas: no one will live there (49:18, 33), a heart like a woman in labor (49:22, 24), and fortunes turned (49:6, 39).
readings: Read as history
Each oracle matches what is known of Babylon's reach: Ammon and Edom subdued, Damascus and Syria taken, Arabs raided in 599/598 BC, and Elam absorbed into Persia.
Read as literature
A catalogue of images: the hidden orphan (49:11), the lion on the Jordan (49:19), the bow broken (49:35). The doom is stated in formulas.
Read as an anthology
Some of the poems (Damascus, Edom) reuse older lines from Amos and Obadiah and were edited together.

views.H: Ammon and Edom lay east of the Jordan and south of the Dead Sea, where Judean refugees fled (40:11). Edom was later displaced by the Nabateans, and the Edomites moved into southern Judea as Idumeans; Herod the Great came from them. Kedar's tribes are named in Assyrian records. Elam passed into Persian control.
views.C: Obadiah 1-9 and Jeremiah 49:7-22 share a text, and scholars divide on which came first. The Greek lacks 49:6 and has Elam at 25:14-19 (Swete numbering). The oracles against Damascus mention Hamath and Arpad, which fell in 720 and 740 BC, so some think the oracle has older roots.
views.J: The Talmud says Obadiah was a convert from Edom (Sanhedrin 39b).
views.X: Acts 2:9 names Elamites at Pentecost, which some connect with Elam's promise in 49:39.
views.F: Some futurist readers see Edom and Ammon as present-day Jordan; others point out that Edom as a people disappeared in antiquity.

deep.b:
The Edom oracle (49:7-22) overlaps Obadiah, the shortest book of the Prophets. The Plain gives them the same wording where the Hebrew is the same; this page treats Jeremiah as the base.

JeremiahObadiah
Jeremiah 49:14 (a report from the LORD; an envoy to the nations)Obadiah 1
Jeremiah 49:15 (small among the nations)Obadiah 2
Jeremiah 49:16 (pride; cracks of the cliff; the high nest)Obadiah 3-4
Jeremiah 49:9 (grape harvesters; thieves)Obadiah 5
Jeremiah 49:10 (Esau stripped bare)Obadiah 6
Jeremiah 49:7 (wisdom in Teman)Obadiah 8

The order differs: Jeremiah has the wisdom verse first and the eagle's nest last; Obadiah opens with the report and ends with the wise men. Three explanations: Obadiah borrowed from Jeremiah; Jeremiah borrowed from Obadiah; both used an older Edom oracle. Obadiah also mentions Jerusalem's fall (verses 11-14), which is not in Jeremiah's version.

deep.title: A circuit around Judah
deep.b: Read in the Hebrew order, the oracles of 46-49 go around Judah like a clock: Egypt (southwest), Philistia (west), Moab, Ammon, Edom (east and south), Damascus (north), Kedar and Hazor (the eastern desert) and Elam (far east), and then comes Babylon (50-51), the power that drives them all. This is Claude's reading of the order, to see how the Hebrew editor arranged it; the Greek's different order (Elam first, Babylon next) would give another picture. The list of nations in 25:19-26 is similar but not in the same order, so the circuit is a suggestion, not a pattern the text announces.

echoes: Obadiah 1-9; Amos 1:3-15; Genesis 19:25; Jeremiah 25:15-26; Jeremiah 50:40; Jeremiah 50:44-46; Acts 2:9; Isaiah 21:13-17

settings.to: Judah, and perhaps the Judean refugees who fled to Ammon (40:11)
settings.when: Undated. Ammon joined the conspiracy of 27:3, and later its king Baalis sent Ishmael against Gedaliah (40:14; 41:15)
settings.why: The question 'Does Israel have no heirs?' says that Ammon is holding land that belongs to Gad. It reassures Israel that its land is not forgotten.
settings.readers: After 586 it spoke to exiles who had lost land to neighbors such as Ammon.

settings.to: Judah, who knew Edom as a 'brother' nation; Edom is not a hearer
settings.when: Undated. Edom was in the conspiracy of 27:3. Lamentations 4:21-22 and Psalm 137:7 remember Edom's behavior when Jerusalem fell
settings.why: Edom was proud of its wisdom and its cliff fortresses. The oracle tells Judah that neither will protect it, and that the sentence of the cup (49:12) reaches Edom, not only Judah.
settings.readers: After 586, with Edom's role in Jerusalem's fall in mind (Obadiah 10-14), it read as justice.
views: Obadiah copied Jeremiah
Obadiah 1-9 is later and has used Jeremiah.
Jeremiah copied Obadiah
Jeremiah has used Obadiah, or an earlier form of it.
Both copied an older oracle
The common source was an earlier oracle against Edom.

settings.to: Judah; Damascus is not a hearer
settings.when: Undated; Hamath and Arpad fell to Assyria in 720 and 740 BC, and Damascus in 732 BC, so the language is older than Jeremiah, unless it describes Babylon's arrival in Syria after 605
settings.why: It shows Syria shaken by bad news, as Judah soon would be. Damascus had once been Israel's enemy.
settings.readers: Exiles saw it fulfilled in the Babylonian conquest of Syria.

settings.to: Judah; the Arabs are not the hearers
settings.when: The heading says the nations were those Nebuchadnezzar attacked; the Babylonian Chronicle reports a raid on the Arabs in 599/598 BC
settings.why: It shows the desert people, who thought themselves out of reach, being plundered. The tribes live without city walls or gates (49:31); the message to Judah is that no one is beyond Babylon.
settings.readers: Exiles who remembered the Babylonian raid in the desert read this as fulfilled.

settings.to: Judah; Elam is far away and not a hearer
settings.when: Early in the reign of Zedekiah, 597/596 BC (49:34)
settings.why: Elam was the farthest power Judah knew. The oracle says Babylon's reach, or the LORD's, covers all lands, and that even Elam's scattering has an end.
settings.readers: After Cyrus came out of old Elamite lands, the oracle read as a distant echo.
views: Fulfilled in the Babylonian era
Elam fell to Babylon and Persia.
Not fulfilled by any known event
Elam's disappearance was gradual and no one event matches the picture.
